title: When the Count Could Not Describe the Pain
source: Author's The Life Between Diagnoses, revised 15 October 2026

scenes.text: The worst mornings could begin with a glass of water. I needed to drink. Sometimes my stomach would not let me keep even that down.
After enough attacks I thought I could predict the eosinophil count from the pain. I knew the guess was not a blood test. But I knew the feeling.
I was sixteen when I finished high school. My father had died, and I had missed much of the year through illness. Medicine was the course I wanted. My grades would not take me there.
At the hospital, medical students came to ask about my case. I did not resent their questions. But when a teaching session ended, I was still the patient in the bed.
A blood count could be precise and still leave things out. Tissue inflammation, a laboratory result, and the ability to eat breakfast are three different questions.
I went on to study chemistry. It became serious work that I chose, not some carefully arranged gift from an illness I would rather not have had.
In 2012 I wrote about the disease online. Years later other people found those words and asked whether ordinary life with an eosinophilic illness could be possible.
Medical names changed as research improved. At one point, serious blood diseases were investigated and later excluded. Relief did not mean the eosinophilic illness had disappeared.
One week before a trip to the United States, another flare brought me to an endoscopy and systemic treatment. Those were responses to an actual attack, not precautions for travelling.
Glucocorticoids could control inflammation, but long treatment had burdens of its own. When I stopped them too abruptly, I developed adrenal insufficiency. My adrenal function later recovered.

I read studies with the training of a pharmaceutical scientist and the memory of those mornings. Histology, symptoms and real-world function belong together; no single endpoint can replace the others.
I do not need my illness turned into a motivational lesson. I want time for the work I choose—and an ordinary morning when a glass of water is only a glass of water.
